questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which king became the first Stuart monarch of England in 1603?
questions.hint: He was already King James VI of Scotland before taking the English throne.
questions.explanation: James I (also James VI of Scotland) succeeded Elizabeth I in 1603, uniting the crowns of England and Scotland and starting the Stuart dynasty.

questions.prompt: Roughly what percentage of those executed for witchcraft in early modern Europe were women?

questions.prompt: Which of these were common reasons women were accused of witchcraft in the 17th century? (Select all that apply)
options: Being a widow or living alone
answer: Being a widow or living alone
questions.hint: Think about who was most vulnerable in village communities.
questions.explanation: Vulnerable women — especially widows, beggars, those with pets ('familiars'), or those involved in disputes — were the most common targets. University education was reserved for men.

questions.explanation: Matthew Hopkins called himself the 'Witchfinder General' and was responsible for around 300 executions during the English Civil War period.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which of these is the BEST explanation for why witch hunts increased during the 1640s in England?
options: The English Civil War caused fear, breakdown of order and economic hardship
Catholics were taking over the country
questions.answer: The English Civil War caused fear, breakdown of order and economic hardship
questions.hint: Times of crisis often produce scapegoats.
questions.explanation: The English Civil War (1642–51) caused massive upheaval — bad harvests, disease, lawlessness and fear made communities look for scapegoats, and witches were a common target.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Witch Craze

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the Gunpowder Plot of 1605?
options: A plan to blow up Parliament and kill King James I
A peasant uprising in the north
A plot to steal the crown jewels
questions.answer: A plan to blow up Parliament and kill King James I
questions.hint: Remember, remember the 5th of November.
questions.explanation: Catholic conspirators led by Robert Catesby (with Guy Fawkes guarding the gunpowder) tried to blow up the House of Lords to kill King James I. The plot was discovered and the plotters executed.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Stuart Era

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Who was the most famous member of the Gunpowder Plot, caught guarding the gunpowder in the cellars of Parliament?
questions.hint: Effigies of him are burned every 5th November.
questions.explanation: Guy Fawkes (also called Guido) was a Catholic soldier caught in the cellars with the gunpowder. He's the figure burned on bonfires every November.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the 'Age of Exploration'?
options: A period when European explorers travelled the world by sea (roughly 1400s–1600s)
The age when railways were built
A period of wars between England and France
When humans first went into space
questions.answer: A period when European explorers travelled the world by sea (roughly 1400s–1600s)
questions.hint: Think Columbus, Magellan, Drake.
questions.explanation: The Age of Exploration was the period from roughly the 1400s to the 1600s when European countries sent ships across the world's oceans, claiming new lands and trade routes.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Age of Exploration

questions.explanation: Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492 while trying to find a westward route to Asia. He never realised he'd reached a continent unknown to Europe.

questions.prompt: What was the name of the first permanent English colony in North America, founded in 1607?

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was the Mayflower?
options: A ship that carried Pilgrim settlers from England to America in 1620
A spice ship from the East Indies
A warship in the Spanish Armada
A pirate vessel captained by Francis Drake
questions.answer: A ship that carried Pilgrim settlers from England to America in 1620
questions.hint: It carried Puritan separatists seeking religious freedom.
questions.explanation: The Mayflower carried around 100 Puritan separatists (the Pilgrims) from Plymouth to New England in 1620. They were seeking freedom to practise their religion.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Which of these were consequences of European exploration of the Americas for indigenous peoples? (Select all that apply)
options: Loss of land and forced removal
Improvement in their economy through trade
answer: Loss of land and forced removal
questions.hint: Four of these were catastrophic; one is a modern misconception.
questions.explanation: European contact was disastrous for indigenous populations — diseases like smallpox killed up to 90% of some communities, and survivors faced land theft, enslavement and cultural destruction.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: How might the actions of King James I have made witch hunts more dangerous in England after 1603?
options: His book Daemonologie gave royal authority to the belief that witches were real and should be hunted
He passed laws protecting accused women
questions.answer: His book Daemonologie gave royal authority to the belief that witches were real and should be hunted
questions.hint: Royal endorsement made witch hunting seem legitimate.
questions.explanation: Because the king himself had written that witchcraft was real and dangerous, judges and ordinary people took accusations more seriously. The Witchcraft Act of 1604 also strengthened punishments.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Witch Craze

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What is the 'Columbian Exchange'?
options: The transfer of plants, animals, people, diseases and ideas between the Old and New Worlds after 1492
A peace treaty between England and Spain
An exchange of prisoners after a war
questions.answer: The transfer of plants, animals, people, diseases and ideas between the Old and New Worlds after 1492
questions.hint: Named after Christopher Columbus.
questions.explanation: The Columbian Exchange describes the massive movement of crops (potatoes, tomatoes, maize), animals (horses, cattle), people, ideas — and tragically diseases — between Europe, Africa and the Americas after 1492.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Age of Exploration

questions.explanation: Potatoes, tomatoes, maize, chocolate and chillies all came from the Americas. Wheat and rice were Old World crops taken to the Americas.

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: What was a 'familiar' in the context of witch beliefs in the 17th century?
options: An animal companion thought to be a demon helper
questions.answer: An animal companion thought to be a demon helper
questions.hint: Often a cat, toad or hare.
questions.explanation: A familiar was an animal — often a cat, dog, toad or hare — believed to be a demon serving a witch. Many lonely women owning pets were accused for this reason.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Witch Craze

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why might historians describe the witch craze as an example of 'scapegoating'?
options: Because vulnerable people were blamed for problems that had other real causes (disease, bad harvests, war)
Because goats were used in witch trials
questions.answer: Because vulnerable people were blamed for problems that had other real causes (disease, bad harvests, war)
questions.hint: A scapegoat is someone unfairly blamed for the problems of others.
questions.explanation: Scapegoating means unfairly blaming someone for problems they didn't cause. When crops failed, children died or disease spread, communities often blamed isolated, vulnerable women rather than face the real causes.
questions.source: CHS Y8 History KM, Autumn — Witch Craze

questions.subject: history
questions.prompt: Why was control of the seas so important to European nations during the Age of Exploration?
options: Sea travel was the fastest way to move goods, soldiers and settlers; controlling sea routes meant controlling trade and empire
Because all gold was found at sea
Because there were no roads in Europe
questions.answer: Sea travel was the fastest way to move goods, soldiers and settlers; controlling sea routes meant controlling trade and empire
questions.hint: Empires were built on shipping lanes.
questions.explanation: Ships were the fastest and most effective way to project power and move trade goods. Nations like Spain, Portugal and later Britain and the Netherlands competed fiercely for naval dominance.
questions.source: UK NC KS3 — Age of Exploration
